\begin{theorem}[Shift invariance; ordered claim false for every $N$]\label{thm:shift}
For all $c,u\in U$, $\Sigma_c(5u)=\Sigma_c(u)$ and $5u\neq u$. Consequently, for every $c$ there exist $u\neq v$ in $U$ with $\Sigma_c(u)=\Sigma_c(v)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $5=1+4$. Then $\Sigma_c(5u)=\Sigma_c(u)+u\cdot 4(1+c)=\Sigma_c(u)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:pairsum}. Also $5u-u=4u\neq 0$ since $u$ is odd.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Zero information for $N\equiv 3\pmod 4$]\label{thm:zero}
If $c\in\{3,7\}$ then $\Sigma_c$ is constant on $U$: equal to $4$ for $c=3$ and to $0$ for $c=7$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$1+c\in\{4,8\}$, and $4u\equiv 4$ and $8u\equiv 0 \pmod 8$ for odd $u$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Classification]\label{thm:class}
$c\in U$ is unordered sum-sufficient if and only if $c=5$. In particular exactly one of the four classes of $N\bmod 8$ is sum-sufficient.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $c=5$ the fibres of $\Sigma_5$ are $\{1,5\}$ and $\{3,7\}$, and $\sigma_5$ swaps $1\leftrightarrow 5$ and $3\leftrightarrow 7$. For $c=1$, $\sigma_1=\mathrm{id}$ and $\Sigma_1(1)=\Sigma_1(5)$. For $c\in\{3,7\}$, $\Sigma_c$ is constant, and any $v\notin\{1,c\}$ violates sufficiency.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Prime counterexample]\label{prop:primes}
The numbers $17,41,5,13$ are prime. Moreover $17\cdot 41\equiv 5\cdot 13$ and $17+41\equiv 5+13\pmod 8$, while $17\not\equiv 5$ and $17\not\equiv 13\pmod 8$, and $17\cdot 41\not\equiv 5\cdot 13\pmod{32}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$697\equiv 65\equiv 1$ and $58\equiv 18\equiv 2\pmod 8$. The factor classes are $\{1,1\}$ and $\{5,5\}$. Finally $697\equiv 25$ and $65\equiv 1\pmod{32}$.
\end{proof}

A prime $\equiv 1\pmod 8$ splits completely in $\Q(\zeta_8)$ and a prime $\equiv 5\pmod 8$ does not. The two semiprimes thus have identical data $(N\bmod 8,s\bmod 8)=(1,2)$ but different $D_4@8$ type pairs.

\begin{proposition}[The symbol contrast, corrected]\label{prop:signs}
If $a,b,a',b'\in\{\pm 1\}$ and $a+b=a'+b'$, then $(a,b)=(a',b')$ or $(a,b)=(b',a')$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The sums $2,0,-2$ correspond exactly to the unordered pairs $\{1,1\},\{1,-1\},\{-1,-1\}$.
\end{proof}

\section{The precision law}\label{sec:law}

\begin{lemma}[Valuation pigeonhole]\label{lem:pigeon}
Let $\ell$ be a prime and $a,b\ge 0$. If $\ell^{a+b+1}\mid xy$, then $\ell^{a+1}\mid x$ or $\ell^{b+1}\mid y$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Induct on $a$. If $\ell\nmid x$, then $\ell^{a+b+1}$ is coprime to $x$, so $\ell^{a+b+1}\mid y$. If $\ell\mid x$ and $a=0$ we are done. Otherwise write $x=\ell x'$, cancel one factor of $\ell$, and apply the induction hypothesis to $\ell^{(a-1)+b+1}\mid x'y$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Vieta identity]\label{lem:vieta}
In any commutative ring,
\[(p-p')(p-q')=p\bigl[(p+q)-(p'+q')\bigr]+\bigl[p'q'-pq\bigr].\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Direct expansion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Precision law]\label{thm:law}
Let $\ell$ be a prime, $k\ge 0$, and suppose $p+q\equiv p'+q'$ and $pq\equiv p'q'\pmod{\ell^k}$. Then $(p,q)$ and $(p',q')$ agree as unordered pairs modulo $\ell^{\ceilhalf{k}}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $c=\ceilhalf{k}$. The case $c=0$ is trivial. Otherwise write $c=a+1$, so that $2a+1\le k$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:vieta}, $\ell^{a+a+1}$ divides $(p-p')(p-q')$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:pigeon}, $\ell^c\mid p-p'$ or $\ell^c\mid p-q'$. In the first case $q-q'=[(p+q)-(p'+q')]-(p-p')$ is divisible by $\ell^c$, since $c\le k$. The second case is symmetric.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness]\label{thm:sharp}
Let $\ell$ be a prime and $c\ge 0$. Put $p=1$, $q=1-2\ell^c$, $p'=q'=1-\ell^c$. Then $p+q=p'+q'$, $pq\equiv p'q'\pmod{\ell^{2c}}$, and neither $p\equiv p'$ nor $p\equiv q'\pmod{\ell^{c+1}}$. For $\ell=2$ and $c\ge 1$ all four numbers are odd.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Both sums equal $2-2\ell^c$. Also $p'q'-pq=\ell^{2c}$, and $p-p'=\ell^c$ is not divisible by $\ell^{c+1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Taking $c=\ceilhalf{k}$, so that $2c \ge k$, shows that the exponent in Theorem~\ref{thm:law} is optimal for every prime and every $k$. Exhaustive enumeration over residue pairs confirms that the determined precision is exactly $\ceilhalf{k}$ for $\ell=2$, $k\le 7$; $\ell=3$, $k\le 4$; and $\ell=5$, $k\le 3$. Heuristically, the roots $\tfrac12(s\pm\sqrt{s^2-4N})$ nearly coincide when the discriminant is highly divisible by $\ell$, and a perturbation of size $\ell^k$ moves them by about $\ell^{k/2}$.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Exact Vieta]\label{thm:exact}
In an integral domain, if $p+q=p'+q'$ and $pq=p'q'$, then $(p,q)=(p',q')$ or $(p,q)=(q',p')$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:vieta}, $(p-p')(p-q')=0$. Hence $p=p'$ or $p=q'$, and the sum gives the other coordinate.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Hensel regime]\label{thm:hensel}
Let $\ell$ be a prime and suppose $\ell\nmid p-q$. If $p+q\equiv p'+q'$ and $pq\equiv p'q'\pmod{\ell^k}$, then $(p,q)$ and $(p',q')$ agree as unordered pairs modulo $\ell^k$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $k\ge 1$, $\ell^k\mid (p-p')(p-q')$. If $\ell$ divided both factors, then $\ell$ would divide $p-q=(p-p')+(p-q')-[(p+q)-(p'+q')]$. So one factor is prime to $\ell$, and $\ell^k$ divides the other. Conclude as in Theorem~\ref{thm:law}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Dyadic obstruction]\label{prop:dyadic}
If $p,q$ are odd then $2\mid p-q$. Odd pairs are therefore never $2$-separated.
\end{proposition}

\section{Consequences for the $D_4@8$ dial}\label{sec:d4}

The $D_4@8$ type of $p$ depends on $p\bmod 2^3$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:law} requires $\ceilhalf{k}\ge 3$, that is $k\ge 5$.

\begin{corollary}[Modulus $32$ suffices]\label{cor:32}
If $p+q\equiv p'+q'$ and $pq\equiv p'q'\pmod{32}$, then $(p,q)$ and $(p',q')$ agree as unordered pairs modulo $8$, and therefore have the same unordered $D_4@8$ type pair.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Modulus $16$ does not]\label{cor:16}
We have $1+9\equiv 13+13$ and $1\cdot 9\equiv 13\cdot 13\pmod{16}$, but $1\not\equiv 13$ and $9\not\equiv 13\pmod 8$. The classes mod $8$ are $\{1,1\}$ and $\{5,5\}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[Numerical illustration]
For $3000$ random semiprimes with $20$-bit factors, the fraction whose unordered type pair $\{p\bmod 8,q\bmod 8\}$ is pinned within the sample by $(s,N)\bmod 2^k$ was about $24\%$ for $k=3$, $75\%$ for $k=4$, and $100\%$ for all $k\ge 5$. The values below $k = 5$ are empirical; the value at $k \ge 5$ is guaranteed by Corollary~\ref{cor:32}.
\end{remark}

The measured $100\%$ sum-carried fraction for $D_4@8$ is therefore incompatible with a channel that reveals only $s\bmod 8$. It must come from sum information modulo $32$ or finer, for example the exact integer sum.

\begin{algorithm}[Pair-sum classifier modulo $8$]
Given $c=N\bmod 8$, compute $\Sigma_c(u)=u(1+c)\bmod 8$ and the partner $cu\bmod 8$ for $u\in U$. Group the $u$ by $\Sigma_c(u)$. Return ``sufficient'' iff each group is contained in $\{u,cu\}$. Cost $O(1)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:class} the output is ``sufficient'' iff $c=5$.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[Determined-precision oracle]
Given $\ell,k$, enumerate $0\le p\le q<\ell^k$ (optionally only separated pairs), bucket them by $(p+q,pq)\bmod\ell^k$, and return the largest $j\le k$ such that every bucket has a single image among unordered pairs modulo $\ell^j$. Cost $O(k\,\ell^{2k})$. The output is $\ceilhalf{k}$ unfiltered and $k$ on separated pairs.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[Unordered pair recovery]
Given $(s,n)\bmod\ell^k$ coming from a true pair, find any $p\bmod\ell^k$ with $p^2-sp+n\equiv 0\pmod{\ell^k}$, and output $\{p,s-p\}\bmod\ell^{\ceilhalf{k}}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:law} the output does not depend on which solution is found. When the true pair is separated, the output is correct modulo $\ell^k$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:hensel}.
\end{algorithm}

\section{Discussion}

An experiment on six "dials" (prime-indexed splitting-type maps of number fields with Galois groups $S_3, A_4, D_4, F_{20}, C_5$) found that the answer depends on the dial. > *"$(p+q) \bmod 8$ determines $p \bmod 8$ and $q \bmod 8$ uniquely, because $q \equiv N p^{-1} \pmod 8$."*

This page shows why that sentence is false and what the correct law is.

<details><summary>Background: what is a "dial"?</summary>

A dial assigns to each prime $p$ its *splitting type* in a fixed number field $K$, meaning how the ideal $(p)$ factors in $K$. By [Chebotarev's density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev%27s_density_theorem) the types are equidistributed according to conjugacy classes of the Galois group. For $D_4@8$ the field sits inside $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_8)$, the field of [eighth roots of unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclotomic_field), so the type of $p$ depends only on $p \bmod 8$. A prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod 8$ splits completely; $p \equiv 5$ does not.
</details>

## 1. The table that breaks the explanation

Every odd residue mod 8 squares to 1, since $(\mathbb{Z}/8)^\times \cong C_2 \times C_2$ is the [Klein four-group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klein_four-group). So with $c = N \bmod 8$ and $u = p \bmod 8$ the partner is $q \equiv cu$, and

$$p + q \equiv u + cu = u(1+c) \pmod 8 .$$

Since $1 + c$ is even, the map $u \mapsto u(1+c)$ cannot be injective on the four odd residues. Explore the full table below: pick $N \bmod 8$, click a cell, and see which other factor classes give the same sum.

## 2. The law that replaces it: precision halving

> **Precision Law.** For every prime $\ell$: if $p+q \equiv p'+q'$ and $pq \equiv p'q' \pmod{\ell^k}$, then $\{p,q\} \equiv \{p',q'\} \pmod{\ell^{\lceil k/2\rceil}}$ as unordered pairs. The exponent $\lceil k/2 \rceil$ is optimal.

The proof uses a single identity (evaluate one quadratic at a root of the other):

$$(p-p')(p-q') = p\,[(p+q)-(p'+q')] + [p'q' - pq] \equiv 0 \pmod{\ell^k}.$$

<details><summary>The valuation pigeonhole and the full proof</summary>

**Lemma.** If $\ell^{a+b+1} \mid xy$ then $\ell^{a+1} \mid x$ or $\ell^{b+1}\mid y$. (Induct on $a$. If $\ell \nmid x$, all of $\ell^{a+b+1}$ divides $y$. Otherwise divide out one $\ell$.)

Apply it with $a = b = \lceil k/2\rceil - 1$, so $a + b + 1 \le k$. One of $p - p'$, $p - q'$ is divisible by $\ell^{\lceil k/2\rceil}$, and the sum congruence transfers this to the other coordinate.

**Sharpness.** $p = 1$, $q = 1 - 2\ell^c$, $p' = q' = 1 - \ell^c$: equal sums, products differing by $\ell^{2c}$, yet $p - p' = \ell^c$ is not divisible by $\ell^{c+1}$.

**Hensel regime.** If $\ell \nmid p - q$, the two factors $p-p'$, $p-q'$ cannot both be divisible by $\ell$, since their sum minus the sum-difference is $p - q$. So all of $\ell^k$ lands on one of them: full precision.

**Exact Vieta.** Over an integral domain, the identity gives $(p-p')(p-q') = 0$, so exact sum and product determine the unordered pair.
</details>
